title: BridgeClear
question: How does a bridge hold weight?
hook: A bridge is just a way of handing weight sideways to the ground. Drag a load across, bend a beam, break an arch, and see why Tacoma Narrows fell for a surprising reason.

explainer.title: Two forces do all the work
explainer.text: Every bridge turns a downward load into compression (squeezing) and tension (stretching). Drag a load across a beam and watch the top turn blue and the bottom red.

explainer.title: Triangles do not bend
explainer.text: A truss keeps only the parts that work. Its triangles cannot change shape without a member changing length, so every stick is simply squeezed or stretched.

explainer.title: An arch turns weight into squeeze
explainer.text: A curve lets stone carry a load in pure compression. The line of thrust runs through the ring, and the abutments must push back against the sideways thrust.

explainer.title: Cables hang, towers stand
explainer.text: A suspension bridge hangs its deck from cables in tension, with towers in compression and huge anchorages at the ends. Cable-stayed bridges run straight stays from tower to deck.

explainer.title: Tacoma was flutter, not simple resonance
explainer.text: In 1940 wind and a twisting deck fed each other until the bridge tore apart. That is aeroelastic flutter. Ordinary resonance stays bounded.

explainer.title: Footsteps, fatigue and floods
explainer.text: The Millennium Bridge swayed when walkers fell into step with it. Cracks grow a little with each load cycle, and floodwater can dig out the ground under a pier.

concepts.def: A squeezing force that pushes the particles of a material together.
A stretching force that pulls the particles of a material apart.
The route a load takes through a structure to the ground.
A rigid frame of straight members joined at their ends, built from triangles.
The path the squeezing force takes through the stones of an arch.
The solid support at each end of an arch or bridge that resists its sideways push.
The curve of a flexible cable hanging under its own weight.
A self-feeding vibration where a structure's motion changes the wind forces that act on it.
When a crowd falls into step with a swaying deck and pushes it harder.
Damage from repeated loading, where a crack grows a little each cycle.
Erosion of the riverbed around a bridge foundation by moving water.
